title: Inclusionary zoning delayed to 2026; Biehn Drive approved
subtitle: Queen Victoria statue report, Grand River Accessibility Advisory Committee appointments, flood-mitigation purchase orders, HR policy updates and regional budget update.
overview: Council's final meeting of 2024 centred on two contested planning items. On inclusionary zoning, Council adopted the planning amendments but set the framework to take effect January 1, 2026, a year later than first planned, and directed staff to report back by the end of 2025 on market conditions and possible adjustments {{vote:m1}}. Supporters of the delay cited weak market conditions; opponents said affordable housing could not wait.

Council also received the Biehn Drive and trunk sanitary sewer environmental study and approved filing it for the provincial 30-day review {{vote:m3}}. The project includes a road extension through part of a provincially significant wetland, which many nearby residents opposed. Staff said Council could only accept or reject the study as a whole.

Council also referred the Queen Victoria statue question to the Arts and Creative Industries Action Plan and ended earlier staff direction on the statue {{vote:m5}}. It approved extra funding for two flood-mitigation projects {{vote:m12}} and appointed a community-agency member to the accessibility advisory committee {{vote:m13}}. The Mayor reported that regional budget committee had voted against three proposed cost shifts to the municipalities, though that budget was not yet final.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the official plan and zoning amendments for inclusionary zoning, to be operational January 1, 2026, with a staff market review due by the end of 2025.
Council received the environmental study report for the Biehn Drive and trunk sanitary sewer extension and directed it be filed with the province for the 30-day review.

Council ended earlier staff direction on the statue and referred a co-led, co-designed commemorative art installation in Victoria Park to the Arts and Creative Industries Action Plan, expected in Q4 2025.

Council increased two Disaster Mitigation and Adaptation Fund purchase orders, for Schneider Creek naturalization and new stormwater facilities, by about $1.02 million and $1.04 million including HST.
Council approved modernized human resources policies, repealed a redundant one, and delegated staff authority to update policies where dates are superseded by negotiated or legislated changes.

Council authorized the General Manager of Infrastructure Services to sign a local improvement petition for the City-owned stormwater facility at 32 Ridgemount Street so staff can keep assessing feasibility.
Council appointed a community-agency representative to the Grand River Accessibility Advisory Committee for a term ending December 31, 2028.
Following a closed session, Council directed staff to proceed as set out in report DSD-2024-508 on the sustainability review of a City-owned arts and culture facility.

debate: On inclusionary zoning, delegates for tenants and housing advocates urged Council to keep the original start date. They said the requirement is small, developers receive many incentives, and delay risks becoming indefinite. Some councillors echoed this and asked why it should wait.

Developer and home builder delegates said high costs, tight lending, and weak condo sales make projects unviable, and that more requirements would reduce supply. Councillors pressed them on interest rates, construction costs, and whether they would build in 2025. Supporters of the amended motion said it commits to a 2026 start and that a later reversal would need a supermajority.

On Biehn Drive, residents raised concerns about wetland loss, road salt near a regional drinking-water well, flooding, emergency access, and whether the traffic study followed guidelines. One delegate argued that the sewer could proceed through a simpler assessment without the road.

Staff said the road would disturb about 0.2% of the wetland and be offset by new wetland, that the traffic study was done by professional engineers, and that source-water protection is a regional responsibility. They said Council could only accept or reject the whole study, and that a separate sewer-only assessment would take about a year. Some councillors cited trust in staff and the planned housing; others said the road was not necessary.

On the Queen Victoria statue, delegates opposed to the staff recommendation called for removing it, saying commemorative art alone was not enough. They said resources for survivors and families were needed. Another delegate supported the proposed commemorative installation.
